title: Hongzhi, Part 4: Wonder
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley returns to Hongzhi's guidepost for silent illumination and its line "Inner illumination restores wonder," closing a sesshin series on that teaching. Eko reads images like dew in the moonlight as a river of stars and weaving gold on a jade loom, then offers examples: sesame seeds from gamasio scattered across the breakfast floor, and the courtroom exchange between a police officer and the mother of the man he shot. Boredom and a self-serving agenda cover wonder, while brief flashes of curiosity, like a single seed that is an uncultivated field, let it appear. Washing the bowl, emptying the self, leads to the Bodhisattva's wonder at one being helping another, and Eko ends with the invitation to stay for the night sit.

sentences.text: Good afternoon.
Energy's a little different in the afternoon, I think, huh?
Does it seem like we just did this?
Here we are.
Even though this is the last talk of the sesshin, it's not a talk about the end of the sesshin.
I'd say it's a talk leading us into our great night of enacting Buddha's enlightenment, and into the great day of the rest of our life, enacting Buddha's manifesting his practice in the world.
Whether we stay some tonight, all tonight, none tonight, our practice is a practice of continuous practice.
And continuous practice enlightenment, there you go.
So day or night, we go forward.
I'd like to offer a few apologies to Hongzhi, I think, just for our...
Well, yes, I'm included.
I'm thinking you want to be included.

So our quick scavenging of Hongzhi's teaching, although reverent scavenging, maybe, I hope we leave you with the impression of wanting to learn more about this very refined teacher and this profound teaching that he has left us, extensive and important in our tradition.
So don't be put off if we have failed to present him in an inspiring light.
I do want to keep this light this afternoon.
I'll try to keep it short.
We're not going to bring forward any new text by Hongzhi, maybe one snippet.
Generally I just want to revisit some of the things we've already looked at, particularly some of the things that Tim brought forth today, because there's plenty there, as we've been noticing.
What I'd like to focus on this afternoon is Hongzhi's teaching, if you can call it a teaching, of wonder.
Returning to wonder.
Restoring wonder as part of his practice of silent illumination.
So what could be lighter than wonder?
Looking at the beginning of the poem that Tim started with, the guidepost for silent illumination:
*Silent and serene, silent and serene, forgetting words, bright clarity appears before you.
When you reflect it, you become vast.
When you embody it, you are spiritually uplifted, spiritually solitary and shining.
Inner illumination restores wonder.
Inner illumination restores wonder.
Dew in the moonlight, a river of stars, snow-covered pines, clouds enveloping the peak.
In darkness it is most bright, while hidden all the more manifest.*
*The crane dreams in the wintry mists.
The autumn waters flow far in the distance.
Endless kalpas are totally empty, all things completely the same.
When wonder exists in serenity, all achievement is forgotten in illumination.
What is this wonder?
Alertly seeing through confusion is the way of silent illumination and the origin of subtle radiance.
Vision penetrating into subtle radiance is weaving gold on a jade loom.*
That's one of Hongzhi's images for putting it all together: weaving gold on a jade loom, in the midst of wonder, which is brought about by inner illumination.
Inner illumination restores wonder.
It was already there, or we already had it, and it's being restored.
So that's what I want to look at this afternoon.
I think we all have some idea of what wonder is, and I would guess we all appreciate it.
Anybody that doesn't like wonder?
Anybody down on wonder?
You've got to like wonder.
Wow, wonder.
It's often associated with children.
I think of the ants crawling on the sidewalk, that kind of thing.
So what else is it?
It's rapt, and it's curious, and it's filled, and it's receptive.
So we kind of know, right?
And children certainly aren't always filled with wonder.
Sometimes they're filled with hunger, and sometimes they're frustrated.
But wonder seems to be restored frequently with young children, right?
We want it to be obscured by something else.
I think wonder perhaps precedes gratitude.
Before gratitude is even born, it's just wonder.
And then, well, here I am, and there is something else, and I am grateful.
I think a child who is struck with wonder is not thinking, oh, I am really lucky.
So it's there, I think, to be restored.
And we're not just talking about wonder for the things that are typically wonderful, right?
We're talking about wonder for the whole works, all the causes and conditions interacting.
Wonder for the things that are not so wonderful as well.
Going back to Hongzhi for a minute: *Dew in the moonlight, a river of stars.* Dew in the moonlight on the grass is literally a river of stars there on the field, a river of stars.
And the river of stars up in the sky literally is simply dew.
It's wonder.
So Hongzhi is pointing to something powerful here, right?
And we can touch it.
We know it.
But so often it's out of reach or out of sight.
So we get the moonlight in the grass and the river of stars, right?
We're plugged into that.
So we have to expand our view of wonder to include all the little inner workings of our lives.
Today, well, I had a wonder experience with gamasio spilled on the floor.
I had a little accident this morning at breakfast.
I bumped the top of that spoon and the gamasio was catapulted onto the floor.
The sesame seeds were dancing.
And I was going, oh my God.
But it was a sight.
There was some wonder there.
It happened like that, right?
And then the wonder of the clean-up drama.
How is the [unclear: "soku"] going to handle that?
I don't know.
But she comes with a cloth and starts working.
The cloth is really dry.
I'm not sure it's going to pick up any of that little salty stuff.
She prevails and order is restored.
And no beans were obstructed.
So the inner workings: there's wonder there, right?
And can we open that even further to the wonder of the human heart that reaches out and loves and is broken, this excruciating wonder?
Can we include that in the river of stars?
I think we can.
Going back to the passage I worked with whenever that was: *Practicing silent illumination, then you reach the great foundation.
Wind blows, moon shines, and beans do not obstruct each other.* As we say, weaving gold on the jade loom.
Can we even expand this wonder to include the story that Tim told at the end of his talk?
The police officer who shot a black man, a white police officer shot a black man.
He was convicted.
And in the courtroom, though, there seemingly was some pretty wonderful encounter with the mother of the victim.
So when we talk about wonder and we talk about beans not obstructing each other, we're not saying that everything is for the best, that everything is as it should be.
We're not saying that.
But we're saying this amazing interaction of beans and energies and constructs and love, weaving the gold, is something that can inspire wonder in us.
And we have the capacity to actually help in these situations.
It's part of that wonder, right?
That exchange, how does that happen?
Beans enter, interact, something opens and something is upheld.
So how is it though that wonder is obscured so much of the time for us?
That's worth looking at, right?
I think it has a lot to do with our preoccupation with our own agenda, right?
Our agenda of getting what this self needs to feel safe and keeping away what this self doesn't like.
We operate with this agenda.
It's far-reaching and it's deep.
And when that agenda arises, I think wonder flees, right?
Because that river of stars really doesn't serve our agenda.
Or if we start to make it serve our agenda, like, oh wow, that's good, I'm going to remember this and put it in a talk or whatever, put it in a poem, then I think wonder has departed, right?
So wonder doesn't serve our agenda.
So much of our waking life, so much of our mental energy, is wrapped up in that agenda.
And I think we all see that.
It's not just a me-first agenda.
It's finding ways to believe, it's preserving my identity.
It's trying not to be afraid.
It's moving towards what I like, distancing myself from what I don't like.
I don't need to dwell on that, right?
We know that.
It's bad enough, right?
But the wonder is there also.
So our agenda intervenes.
I think, though, that throughout our day we have little flashes of disinterested curiosity, right?
Like, oh, what's that?
It might be wrapped up in some part of our agenda, but something will catch our eye.
And for a moment we'll just be, oh, curious.
It's like the agenda disappears, and there's this moment of wonder.
And maybe quickly then the agenda reasserts itself and says I don't have time to look at this little thing, or this is not important, this doesn't affect me.
And we move on to something that seems important, right?
But these little flashes, what I'm calling disinterested curiosity, that is interested: it doesn't interest our agenda-driven self, but something attracts our attention.
Something draws us to it.
So these little flashes, I think, are wonder trying to make an appearance in our life.
And little doorways perhaps, or seeds even.
It just so happens that Hongzhi has this beautiful little image of a single seed as an uncultivated field.
A single seed is an uncultivated field, or something there.
A single flash of curiosity is a field of wonder revealing itself.
A single seed.
Let me just read a little bit more of that passage:
*Directly arriving here you will be able to recognize the mind-ground Dharma field that is the root source of the 10,000 forms germinating with unwithered fertility.
These flowers and leaves are the whole world.*
So we are told that a single seed is an uncultivated field.
This uncultivated field, as is suggested here, is this field of emptiness, which is also the field of unwithered fertility, the root source of the 10,000 forms.
So certainly the natural response would be wonder.
Our natural response.
So I think it comes in.
Those sesame seeds dancing on the floor, I might have been a little bit shocked, but it comes into our lives.
Our agenda, I think we've probably become more familiar with that over the course of the last couple days.
Oh yeah, this is that again, that again.

So the practice of silent illumination I think suggests enlarging that field: illuminating the agenda for what it is and enlarging the field so that it includes many other things, and has room for many other things, including wonder.
Another way we might notice that wonder is obscured, we call it boredom sometimes.
Isn't this wonderful?
No, it's really kind of boring.
I'm not really interested.
So what is that response?
It's one of my favorite topics because it seems like there's a lot there.
I think when we're bored we're suffering because we have this agenda that we're holding unconsciously and it's not getting met.
Or something's bothering us and we're not being distracted.
You can investigate for yourself.
But I think boredom is something we can notice that comes in and obscures wonder.
So what does Hongzhi say about returning to wonder?
What other practical suggestions does he have?
Well, I think the passage that Tim worked with this morning is very helpful.
Wash your bowls.
Empty out the self so that you won't be full of the self.
And what does that mean?
Discover what that means.
I think one way to discover it is that when the self is emptied out, then wonder is restored.
When the bowls are washed.
We can find the self.
And again, it's not dumping our bowl into the garbage compactor and smashing it up and sealing it up and sending it somewhere.
It's really just emptying it into the larger field so that we are open and receptive and can be filled with wonder.
We talk about being filled with wonder.
We can't be filled with wonder if we are full of our self, our agenda.
Let's look at that passage one more time as well:
*Traveling the world, meeting conditions, the self joyfully enters samadhi in all delusions and accepts its function, which is to empty out the self so as not to be full of itself.*
Whether we accept that as our most basic function or not, we can see that that's a practice that leads to wonder, I think.
*Empty out the self so as not to be full of the self.
The empty valley receives the clouds.
The cold stream cleanses the moon.
Despite a hundred uglinesses or a thousand stupidities, the upright cauldron is naturally of benefit.* Zhaozhou's *answers, wash out your bowl, drink your tea.
Do not require making arrangements.* We don't have to set up a big thing.
We just, please wash your bowls, drink your tea.
*From the beginning they have always been perfectly apparent.
Thoroughly observing each thing with the whole eye is the Patra Monk's spontaneous conduct.*
That's really nice, I think.
Thoroughly observing each thing with the whole eye is our spontaneous conduct when we are unfettered by our agenda, perhaps.
Wash your bowls.
Empty out the self.
This whole eye that is the spontaneous conduct, the Patra Monk, is your eye, my eye.
Somehow it's wonderful.
Somehow it's penetrating.
It penetrates the mist.
It's like wonder has this penetrating quality and it also has this quality of filling us with light.
Finally we come, as I suggested before, to that ultimate wonder of the Bodhisattva helping another being.
The aspiring Bodhisattva, of course, is us.
So what is the wonder there?
What is that exchange?
What is given and what is received?
When that little drama in the courtroom, the policeman says, I'm sorry, and the mother responds, I know.
Is that exchange there?
What comes together?
What is let go of?
These workings are nothing other than wonder.
And so the Bodhisattva, I think, plays in this field of wonder.
And that's our aspiration, right?
To return to this open, bright field and live in wonder.
Live as a Bodhisattva, which includes all of our stuff, right?
So that agenda, which is all wrapped in itself and having a conversation with itself over in the corner, but in the larger field there's the river of stars.
I am so happy to be doing this with all of you and seeing that little bit of wonder and witnessing it fill the sky.
Seeing how one being helps another and the whole world breaks open.
And we do this continuously too, right?
We're doing it.
It's happening.
We're in the middle of it.
And there's no end to it.
So tonight some of us will stay a little bit late.
Some of us might stay quite late and sit into the night and re-enact, maybe actualize, this return to wonder.
Or not.
Some of us will have had enough by nine o'clock and will choose to go home to bed or wherever our bed is, and come back in the morning and still continue to practice.
All modes of practice are honored.
We invite you to try the night, but you may have already had enough of the night by the time nine o'clock rolls around.
We'll give you some details about that later in the day.
For now I want to do this again.
Hold you all.
Say thank you.
